title: Adaptive resilience from genes to ecosystems: integrating evolutionary and ecological dynamics
content:
Abstract
Resilience in biological systems emerges from interactions operating across hierarchical levels, from molecular regulation to ecosystem dynamics. Although resilience has traditionally been studied at ecosystem or community scales, fewer studies integrate mechanistic organismal processes with broader ecological outcomes within a unified mathematical framework. Here, I developed a multiscale theoretical and simulation framework linking genetic adaptation, cellular homeostasis, physiological energy allocation, demographic dynamics, species interactions, and ecosystem stability. Deterministic simulations were complemented with stochastic perturbations to evaluate system responses under environmental variability. The framework uses differential equation models describing allele-frequency change, homeostatic regulation, logistic population growth, generalized Lotka–Volterra dynamics, and biodiversity–resilience relationships. Stochasticity was introduced through environmental fluctuations to assess behaviour under uncertainty. Simulations showed divergence between resilient and vulnerable taxa under stress, with resilient populations increasing by 176.7% over 20 years, whereas vulnerable populations declined by 45.1%. Ecosystem resilience increased logarithmically with species richness, indicating positive but diminishing stabilizing effects of biodiversity. Cellular and physiological models further showed that resilience depends on regulatory stability and energetic trade-offs among maintenance, reproduction, and repair. This framework provides an integrative multiscale representation of resilience across biological organization, suggesting that resilience emerges from interactions among genetic, physiological, demographic, and ecological processes across scales.
